Stated Claim / Post Context:
South Korea shifts property tax focus to home values

 S. Korea plans to base its property holding tax more heavily on home values and owner occupancy while raising rates on expensive and rent properties.

Actual Article Body:

Aug. 3 (Asia Today) -- South Korea plans to overhaul its comprehensive real estate holding tax by placing greater emphasis on property values and whether owners live in their homes rather than on the number of homes they own.

The government said the changes are intended to reduce taxes for people who live in a single home while raising the burden on expensive and non-owner-occupied properties.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_76034" });

The proposal also targets a practice commonly described in South Korea as owning "one smart home," in which investors concentrate their wealth in a single premium property to receive tax advantages available to single-home owners.

The Ministry of Finance and Economy announced the measures Monday as part of its 2026 tax reform plan.

Deputy Prime Minister and Finance and Economy Minister Koo Yun Cheol said the government wants to establish a housing market centered on residence rather than speculation.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_67822" });

"A house should not simply be something to buy but a place to live," Koo said at a preliminary briefing Wednesday at the government complex in Sejong.

Beginning in 2028, the same tax rates would apply according to the taxable value of property regardless of how many homes a taxpayer owns.

Under the current system, higher rates of 2% to 5% generally apply to owners of at least three homes when their taxable property value exceeds 1.2 billion won ($813,500).

The revised system would apply the higher rates to all taxpayers with properties in the same value brackets, regardless of the number of homes they own.

The rate on taxable property valued between 1.2 billion won and 2.5 billion won ($813,500 to $1.7 million) would rise from 1.3% to 2%.

The rate for property valued between 2.5 billion won and 5 billion won ($1.7 million to $3.4 million) would increase from 1.5% to 3%.

Properties valued between 5 billion won and 9.4 billion won ($3.4 million to $6.4 million) would be taxed at 4%, up from 2%.

The top rate on taxable property exceeding 9.4 billion won ($6.4 million) would rise from 2.7% to 5%.

The government plans to introduce intermediate rates in 2027 before fully implementing the revised schedule in 2028.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_58846" });

Owner-occupants with one home would receive additional protection.

The assessed-value threshold at which a single-home owner becomes subject to the holding tax would rise from 1.2 billion won to 1.4 billion won ($949,000).

The government estimates that the change would exempt owner-occupied homes with market values of about 2 billion won ($1.36 million) or less. The official proposal says taxes would generally decline for owner-occupied homes valued between about 2 billion won and 3 billion won ($1.36 million and $2.03 million), while the burden would increase on many homes valued above approximately 4 billion won to 5 billion won ($2.71 million to $3.39 million).

The basic deduction for an owner who lives in a single home would increase to 1.4 billion won ($949,000). The deduction for a single home in which the owner does not reside would be reduced to 900 million won ($610,000).

The government expects taxes to begin rising for some homes with market values of about 3.5 billion won ($2.37 million), with larger increases affecting properties worth more than approximately 4.6 billion won ($3.12 million).

The fair market value ratio used to calculate taxable property would also rise gradually from the current 60%.

Owners of at least three homes and people holding property in government-designated regulated areas would face a ratio of up to 80% by 2028
